ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Surgical Oncology (breast) Referral — Richard Roundtree — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: New painless lump under the left nipple in a man of 51

text.paragraph: Man of 51 with a new 1.5 cm firm, painless lump eccentric to the left nipple and a palpable left axillary node; breast cancer suspected. Diagnostic mammography, ultrasound, and core biopsy are booked for tomorrow. Please see him as soon as the results are back to plan surgery. [S]
Urgency: Urgent suspected-cancer pathway, within one week. [S]

list.item: If the biopsy confirms cancer, what is the clinical stage, and does he need staging scans before surgery?
What operation do you recommend for the breast, and how should the axilla be managed if the node is positive?
Should germline testing be done before surgery, and would its result change the operation?
What should he expect after surgery, including drains, shoulder movement, and lymphedema prevention?
Who will plan treatment after surgery, and when?

text.paragraph: He found the lump in the shower a few days ago and at first put it down to the breast enlargement he had at 13. Examination: a 1.5 cm firm, irregular, non-tender mass eccentric to the left nipple at 2 o'clock, not fixed to the chest wall, with no nipple retraction or discharge; one firm, mobile 1 cm left axillary node; the right breast has no mass and no glandular enlargement. The findings are those of a cancer, not gynecomastia, which is usually soft, rubbery, central, and often on both sides. He is otherwise well, takes no regular medicines, never smoked, and drinks two or three times a week. No family history is recorded. He is an actor and is anxious that the diagnosis stay private. PHQ-2 score 1 [S]

list.item: Found a small, painless lump under the left nipple in the shower a few days ago; at first put it down to the breast enlargement he had at 13. [S]
Embarrassed to bring up a breast lump and did not think a man could have breast cancer; worried that a diagnosis could cost him work and wants it kept private. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Richard Roundtree was born on July 9, 1942, in New Rochelle, New York. [D]
Roundtree was an actor best known as the private detective John Shaft in films beginning in the early 1970s, and is described as the first Black action hero. [D]

Roundtree told PEOPLE that at the end of September 1993, in the shower, he felt a lump under his left nipple, 'the size of a lima bean'; he was not overly concerned at first, because at 13 he had had gynecomastia (breast enlargement), and he 'just chalked it up to that.' [D]

In a 2019 television interview Roundtree said he found the lump in the shower while working in Costa Rica in 1993 and saw his doctor after returning to Los Angeles a week later; the doctor biopsied it and four or five days later told him he had breast cancer. Asked whether he had felt shame, he answered 'Embarrassment,' and he said men 'are so cavalier about their health issues and want to sweep it under the rug.' [D]

text.paragraph: 6 later historical claims are omitted because they describe events after the index age. See the teaching note.
No medications started by this date.

tr.td: Invasive ductal carcinoma of the left male breast, central (retroareolar) portion: a 1.5 cm firm, painless lump eccentric to the left nipple at presentation, confirmed by core biopsy the next day; grade 3, ER positive, PR positive, HER2 negative; clinical stage IIA (cT1c cN1 M0), and pathologic stage IIA (pT1c pN1a) after mastectomy and axillary dissection; synthetic modern detail linked to his publicly disclosed breast cancer
S — Synthetic size, grade, receptor status, and stage; the left-sided lump, the operation, and the spread to lymph nodes are from his public account (D).

list.item: Invasive ductal carcinoma of the left male breast, central (retroareolar) portion: a 1.5 cm firm, painless lump eccentric to the left nipple at presentation, confirmed by core biopsy the next day; grade 3, ER positive, PR positive, HER2 negative; clinical stage IIA (cT1c cN1 M0), and pathologic stage IIA (pT1c pN1a) after mastectomy and axillary dissection; synthetic modern detail linked to his publicly disclosed breast cancer: active, confirmed [S]

Same-week diagnostic mammography and ultrasound of both breasts and both axillae, and ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the mass and the abnormal node with ER, PR, and HER2 testing. Guideline: Hassett MJ, et al. Management of Male Breast Cancer: ASCO Guideline. J Clin Oncol 2020;38(16):1849-1863 (2020); NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Breast Cancer, Version 5.2025 (2025) [S]

Genetic counseling and germline multigene panel testing (including BRCA2, BRCA1, PALB2, CHEK2, and ATM), as for every man with breast cancer, with a letter for relatives if a variant is found. Guideline: Hassett MJ, et al. Management of Male Breast Cancer: ASCO Guideline. J Clin Oncol 2020;38(16):1849-1863 (2020); Bedrosian I, et al. Germline Testing in Patients With Breast Cancer: ASCO-Society of Surgical Oncology Guideline. J Clin Oncol 2024;42(5):584-604 (2024) [S]

Mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection, then shoulder exercises and lymphedema risk reduction with arm measurements at each visit. Guideline: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Breast Cancer, Version 5.2025 (2025); Runowicz CD, et al. American Cancer Society/American Society of Clinical Oncology Breast Cancer Survivorship Care Guideline. CA Cancer J Clin 2016;66(1):43-73 (2016) [S]

Adjuvant chemotherapy given by medical oncology (doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide every three weeks for four cycles, then weekly paclitaxel for twelve weeks, about six months), after a baseline echocardiogram, hepatitis B screening, vaccines, and a dental review; radiation oncology review of post-mastectomy radiation after chemotherapy. Guideline: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Breast Cancer, Version 5.2025 (2025); Armenian SH, et al. Prevention and Monitoring of Cardiac Dysfunction in Survivors of Adult Cancers: ASCO Clinical Practice Guideline. J Clin Oncol 2017;35(8):893-911 (2017); Hwang JP, et al. Hepatitis B Virus Screening and Management for Patients With Cancer Prior to Therapy: ASCO Provisional Clinical Opinion Update. J Clin Oncol 2020 (2020) [S]

Tamoxifen after chemotherapy for at least five years, the first-choice endocrine therapy for men, with venous thromboembolism, mood, hot flash, sexual side effect, and adherence checks at every visit. Guideline: Hassett MJ, et al. Management of Male Breast Cancer: ASCO Guideline. J Clin Oncol 2020;38(16):1849-1863 (2020); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, breast cancer monograph (2026) [S]

Distress screening at each visit, plain information that men get breast cancer, confidential handling of his diagnosis at work, and the offer of a peer-support group for men with breast cancer. Guideline: Runowicz CD, et al. American Cancer Society/American Society of Clinical Oncology Breast Cancer Survivorship Care Guideline. CA Cancer J Clin 2016;66(1):43-73 (2016); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, breast cancer monograph (2026) [S]
Referral to surgical oncology (breast), Farah Siddiqui, MD, ordered 1993-09-29 [S]
